### Problem: Longest Cycle in a Graph {#sec-gr-p5-cycle}

`edges[i]` is the unique successor of vertex $i$, or $-1$ when $i$ has none. There is at most one outgoing edge, and there are no self-loops in the official tests. Return the length of the longest cycle, or $-1$ when there is no cycle. $n \le 10^5$.

**Graph model.** A functional graph with missing arcs allowed. A missing arc is a tail that ends.

**Invariants.** `when[v]` is the global time at which $v$ was first stamped, or $-1$. A walk records the time at which it started. Hitting a vertex whose stamp is at least that start means the hit lies on this walk, and the cycle length is `time - when[v]`. A stamp from before this walk is an old component. The best length starts at $-1$, so a graph with no cycle stays $-1$ rather than $0$.

**Approaches.**

1. **Timestamps** — one array, one clock. $O(n)$. This is the form to submit.
2. **Peel** — delete in-degree $0$ until nothing of in-degree $0$ remains. The surviving vertices are disjoint cycles. The longest survivor is the answer.

::: {#fig-gr-p5-cycle}

#### Timestamps

::: {.form-next}
Stamp a vertex at the moment the current walk enters it. Test `v != -1` before reading `when[v]`.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("cycle", "time")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def longest_cycle(edges):
    n = len(edges)
    when = [-1] * n
    time = 0
    best = -1
    for s in range(n):
        if when[s] != -1:
            continue
        start = time
        v = s
        while v != -1 and when[v] == -1:
            when[v] = time
            time += 1
            v = edges[v]
        if v != -1 and when[v] >= start:
            best = max(best, time - when[v])
    return best


def longest_cycle_forget(edges):
    """Counts a hit on any earlier stamp, including a previous component."""
    n = len(edges)
    when = [-1] * n
    time = 0
    best = -1
    for s in range(n):
        if when[s] != -1:
            continue
        v = s
        while v != -1 and when[v] == -1:
            when[v] = time
            time += 1
            v = edges[v]
        if v != -1 and when[v] != -1:
            best = max(best, time - when[v])
    return best


assert longest_cycle([3, 3, 4, 2, 3]) == 3
assert longest_cycle([2, -1, 3, 1]) == -1
assert longest_cycle([1, 0]) == 2
assert longest_cycle([-1]) == -1
assert longest_cycle([1, 0, 1]) == 2
assert longest_cycle([1, 0, 3, 1]) == 2
assert longest_cycle_forget([1, 0, 3, 1]) == 3
```

##### C++

```cpp
int longestCycle(vector<int>& edges) {
    int n = edges.size(), time = 0, best = -1;
    vector<int> when(n, -1);
    for (int s = 0; s < n; s++) {
        if (when[s] != -1) continue;
        int start = time, v = s;
        while (v != -1 && when[v] == -1) {
            when[v] = time++;
            v = edges[v];
        }
        if (v != -1 && when[v] >= start) best = max(best, time - when[v]);
    }
    return best;
}
```

:::

#### Peel

::: {.form-next}
A vertex of in-degree $0$ is not on a cycle. Delete it and decrease its successor. Each remaining component is a pure cycle; walk it once.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("cycle", "peel")
    assert str(final) == "3"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def longest_cycle_peel(edges):
    n = len(edges)
    indeg = [0] * n
    for v in edges:
        if v != -1:
            indeg[v] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
    alive = [True] * n
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        alive[u] = False
        v = edges[u]
        if v != -1:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    best = -1
    seen = [False] * n
    for s in range(n):
        if not alive[s] or seen[s]:
            continue
        length = 0
        v = s
        while not seen[v]:
            seen[v] = True
            length += 1
            v = edges[v]
        best = max(best, length)
    return best


assert longest_cycle_peel([3, 3, 4, 2, 3]) == 3
assert longest_cycle_peel([2, -1, 3, 1]) == -1
assert longest_cycle_peel([1, 0]) == 2
for n in range(1, 10):
    for _ in range(25):
        edges = [random.choice(list(range(n)) + [-1]) for _ in range(n)]
        assert longest_cycle(edges) == longest_cycle_peel(edges)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int longestCyclePeel(vector<int>& edges) {
    int n = edges.size();
    vector<int> indeg(n);
    for (int v : edges)
        if (v != -1) indeg[v]++;
    queue<int> q;
    vector<char> alive(n, 1);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
        if (indeg[i] == 0) q.push(i);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front();
        q.pop();
        alive[u] = 0;
        int v = edges[u];
        if (v != -1 && --indeg[v] == 0) q.push(v);
    }
    int best = -1;
    vector<char> seen(n);
    for (int s = 0; s < n; s++) {
        if (!alive[s] || seen[s]) continue;
        int length = 0, v = s;
        while (!seen[v]) {
            seen[v] = 1;
            length++;
            v = edges[v];
        }
        best = max(best, length);
    }
    return best;
}
```

:::

:::

**Worked trace.** `[3, 3, 4, 2, 3]` enters the cycle at vertex $2$: the successors are $2 \to 4 \to 3 \to 2$, length $3$. `[1, 0, 3, 1]` is a $2$-cycle on $\{0, 1\}$ plus the tail $2 \to 3 \to 1$. Processing $0$ first stamps the cycle. The later walk from $2$ hits a stamp that is older than the walk. Keeping that hit produces length $3$. Rejecting an old stamp leaves the answer at $2$.

**Edge cases.** A single vertex with no arc returns $-1$. A $2$-cycle returns $2$. A chain into a missing arc returns $-1$. The best value starts at $-1$, so "no cycle" and "a cycle of length $0$" are different answers, and only the first occurs.

**Pitfalls.** Reading `when[v]` when `v` is $-1$ is an out-of-range access; the test is `v != -1` first. A boolean "visited" array has no start time, so a tail that falls into a cycle found earlier looks like a new cycle. Initialising the answer to $0$ turns the acyclic sample into a wrong zero.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **A boolean visited array.** It cannot tell this walk from an earlier component. On `[1, 0, 3, 1]` the tail into the old cycle reports length $3$. The test `when[v] >= start` leaves the answer at $2$.
- **A fresh search from every vertex.** One long chain into a cycle makes that quadratic. One `when` array measures every cycle in linear time.
- **The tail counted into the length.** The length is `time - when[v]` at the repeated vertex. The walk from $0$ on `[3, 3, 4, 2, 3]` is longer than the cycle, and the cycle has length $3$.
- **Returning $0$.** A graph with no cycle returns $-1$. Every real cycle has length at least $2$, so $-1$ is not an answer that a cycle can produce.
:::

**Variants.** A permutation has no tails and no missing arc, so a plain seen array measures every cycle: [LC 565 · Array Nesting](https://leetcode.com/problems/array-nesting/){difficulty="Medium"}. The first repeated vertex of every walk is @sec-gr-p5-badge. Counting cycles, rather than measuring the longest, is the same test with a counter in place of the length. Seating people next to their favourite is [LC 2127 · Maximum Employees to Be Invited to a Meeting](https://leetcode.com/problems/maximum-employees-to-be-invited-to-a-meeting/){difficulty="Hard"}: one long cycle, or every 2-cycle extended by the chains into its two ends.

Source: [LC 2360 · Longest Cycle in a Graph](https://leetcode.com/problems/longest-cycle-in-a-graph/){.solved difficulty="Hard"}
